<reason>Both sides argued well, and CON's reframe (the Bismarck-style multi-payer, work-channelled systems in Germany/Japan/NL are universal without a monopoly payer) was the most original move in the debate. But PRO landed the decisive framing on the motion as written: the comparator condemned is employer-based insurance that ties access to work status, and CON's own best model keeps people covered only because the state pays contributions when work stops, regulators force money to follow sick patients, and funds cannot refuse anyone. PRO pressed this consistently ([B2.3], [B3.1], [B4.5], [B5.1]) and CON's reply — that work remains the "default channel" and the financing base — conceded the access tie while trying to convert the motion into a pure one-payer/many-payer question, which is a partial swap of the resolution. PRO also neutralized CON's strongest independent harm (no exit) with the symmetry point that Germany runs its own cost-effectiveness assessments, so switching funds only changes the letterhead on the rejection; CON retreated to exit over referral speed and coordination, a much smaller claim. Crucially, fragmentation overhead and single-buyer bargaining power went essentially unanswered by CON across the whole debate, despite PRO flagging the omission twice. CON's best counter-turn — that if outcomes track funding, the question becomes which structure defends funding best, and earmarked contributions resist cuts better than budget lines — was genuinely sharp, but PRO's "firewall is a fuse" reply (the wage base shrinks exactly when need spikes, and the German backstop already puts the treasury in the loop) blunted it. CON also carried an execution cost from a clipped over-length rebuttal. PRO gave the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 and follow-through: "If losing your job never means losing your doctor, then work is merely the billing address" — forcing CON to admit its universal model severs the very tie the motion condemns, so CON was defending the letter of employer-based insurance while abandoning its substance. PRO's symmetry answer on drug refusals (every fund draws on the same assessment, so switching funds only changes the letterhead) was the second most damaging blow, gutting CON's "abolition of exit" line.</best_rebuttal>
